summary: This informational document updates some auxiliary ASN.1 modules for CMS and PKIX from the 1988 syntax to the 2008 one. The old modules stay normative and the wire formats don't change. This helps tools that prefer the newer notation.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6268 rewrites nine CMS and PKIX ASN.1 modules using the 2008 notation. The older 1988 modules remain the normative definitions, and the message formats on the wire do not change.

questions: do the cms asn.1 modules change on the wire
which rfcs have updated asn.1 modules in rfc 6268
subtitle: Nine CMS and PKIX ASN.1 modules rewritten in 2008 syntax without changing wire formats.

tldr.problem: Many security-related RFCs describe data formats using the 1988 version of ASN.1, while some developers wanted updated module syntax.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6268 supplies 2008-compliant ASN.1 modules for nine earlier RFCs and draws on modules in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912 to make the modules self-contained.
tldr.outcome: The new modules are informative; the 1988 modules remain normative. The document states that the changes do not alter bits on the wire.

today: RFC 6268 is Informational and updates RFC 5911. The RFC states that the original 1988 ASN.1 modules remain normative.

sections.title: Why Update the ASN.1 Modules
sections.content:
Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and related formats are described using ASN.1, a notation for data structures. Many security RFCs still use the 1988 ASN.1 syntax, which had been deprecated, and developers wanted modules using a newer version.

RFC 6268 provides modules compatible with the 2008 ASN.1 specification. It explicitly says the change is syntactic: it makes no bits-on-the-wire changes to the formats.
sections.plainLanguage: The document updates how selected data structures are written down, not how their encoded messages look. Software that reads the wire format sees no format change from this update.

sections.title: The Nine Modules Covered
sections.content:
The modules come from RFCs 3274, 3779, 6019, 4073, 4231, 4334, 5083, 5652, and 5752. They cover CMS compressed data, X.509 IP-address and AS-identifier extensions, BinaryTime, multiple-content protection, HMAC identifiers, WLAN and PPP certificate information, authenticated-enveloped data, CMS, and multiple signatures.

Some definitions are imported from locations different from the originals. Along with the modules in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912, the updated modules can stand on their own without importing definitions from elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: Nine earlier RFCs receive corresponding modules written in the newer notation. Together with the modules in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912, they can be used without additional external definitions.

sections.title: What the Updated Syntax Enables
sections.content:
The 2008 ASN.1 specification includes additional predefined types and encoding-control features, but the new types are not used in the modules published here. One visible change in the CMS modules is separate attribute sets for different content types.

The modules also define a parameterized EncryptedContentInfo type that can be used with different algorithm sets. The RFC says this supports more precise constraints on which attributes apply to which content type while keeping output changes from earlier module versions small.
sections.plainLanguage: The revised syntax lets a module state more precisely which attributes belong with a particular content type. The document does not use the new predefined types it describes.

sections.title: Normative Status and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says the original 1988 ASN.1 syntax remains normative. The modules in RFC 6268, like those in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912, are informative annexes and do not explicitly update the source RFCs from which the modules were taken.

The document discusses a possible separate module for ASN.1 module identifier assignments, which could reduce edits when a module is replaced. The modules in RFC 6268 do not implement that approach. Its security section says the wire formats remain unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier modules remain the official definitions; the new modules are additional references for readers and tools. Since the wire formats stay the same, the document says the modules introduce no new security considerations.
